concept.title: Split one plane-motion event into independent x/y components with one clock
concept.inferential_jump: Perpendicular components may be solved separately because each axis equation contains only that axis's quantities, but they still describe one object at one physical time.
entry_assumptions: Can read signed vector components in a declared x-y frame.

teaching_path.action: Choose one fixed x-y frame, one origin and one time origin for the whole plane-motion event.
teaching_path.why_valid: A component value is meaningful only after its frame and sign convention are fixed.
teaching_path.output: one declared frame, origin, axis orientation and t=0

teaching_path.action: Represent position, velocity and acceleration as signed x and y components in that same frame.
teaching_path.why_valid: A plane vector is completely represented by its perpendicular Cartesian components once the frame is declared.

teaching_path.action: Keep x-quantities in the x description and y-quantities in the y description while using one shared elapsed time.
teaching_path.why_valid: The perpendicular component equations are independent in Cartesian kinematics, but both describe the same object during the same physical interval.
teaching_path.output: two axis histories coupled by one clock

teaching_path.action: Recombine only component values that refer to the same frame and the same instant.
teaching_path.why_valid: Mixing x at one time with y at another does not describe any single physical state of the object.
teaching_path.output: one physically valid plane state reconstructed from simultaneous components

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Independent x and y motions may use different elapsed times.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: At one instant 2 s after launch, may the x equation use t=2 s while the y equation uses another time?
misconceptions.repair: No. Independence separates the axis equations; it does not give the same object two clocks.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The x-motion and y-motion are two different objects that can be paired arbitrarily later.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: May x(2 s) be combined with y(3 s) to describe the particle's position?
misconceptions.repair: No. A plane state is a simultaneous pair. Recombine x(t) and y(t) only at the same t in the same frame.

correspondence.in_words: The horizontal velocity component at the shared physical time.
The vertical velocity component at the same shared physical time.
The one elapsed time used by both component descriptions.

scene.frame: One physical particle in one declared x-y frame; every component sample remains attached to its own sample time.
scene.caption: Same-time x and y samples may reconstruct one simultaneous particle state; mixed-time samples are non-simultaneous and must be rejected.

transactions.summary: Same-time x(2 s) and y(2 s) samples refer to one shared physical instant and may be recombined.

transactions.reason: Mixing x at one time with y at another does not describe any single physical state of the object.

exit_task.prompt: A particle has x-velocity 6 m/s and y-velocity -8 m/s at t=3 s. Explain what 'independent components' means and what must remain shared between the x and y descriptions.

answer.summary: The x and y component equations are solved separately in the same frame, but both describe the same particle at the same t=3 s.
reasoning: Keep x quantities in the x equation and y quantities in the y equation.
Use one common elapsed time for the same physical instant.
Recombine components only after each axis is handled consistently.
answer.check: Both component values must refer to the same frame and same instant.

oracle.no_numeric_claim: No new numerical computation is required.

application.stem: A stone is launched horizontally at 15 m/s from a cliff 20 m above level ground. Take +y upward and g=10 m/s^2. Find the flight time, horizontal range and impact velocity.
conditions: Ground is 20 m below the launch point.

reasoning_route.action: Represent the horizontal and vertical histories in one declared frame with one shared elapsed time, placing the 20 m drop in the vertical component.
reasoning_route.why_valid: The component equations evolve independently but still describe one stone at one physical instant, so the known landing geometry belongs to y while time remains common.
reasoning_route.output: Two component descriptions coupled by one shared event clock.

reasoning_route.action: Use the vertical ground-contact condition Delta y=-20 m to determine the flight time before calculating horizontal range or impact velocity.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Ground impact is defined by the vertical displacement, so the y equation identifies the event time; that one time then belongs to every component at impact.
reasoning_route.output: t_event=2 s is the common impact time.

reasoning_route.action: Reuse t_event=2 s in the horizontal displacement and both velocity components.
reasoning_route.why_valid: Range and impact velocity must be reconstructed at the same physical event that the vertical equation identified.
reasoning_route.output: Delta x=30 m, v_x=15 m/s and v_y=-20 m/s at impact.

reasoning_route.action: Check that the ideal fall time is set by vertical motion while horizontal speed changes the range but not the vertical landing event.
reasoning_route.why_valid: With a_x=0 and no drag, the vertical event equation contains no horizontal speed.
reasoning_route.output: The result is consistent with independent components and one shared clock.

hints.text: Which component equation contains the known 20 m drop?
Find the common impact time from y first, then use that same time in x and in the velocity components.

scaffolds.text: Draw x and y as separate columns tied to one shared t, and place the 20 m drop only in the y column.
Name the physical condition that says the stone has reached the ground before solving for the event time.

application.check: The fall time comes from vertical motion; changing only horizontal speed would change range but not the ideal fall time.

solution.summary: The flight time is 2 s, the horizontal range is 30 m, and the impact velocity is (15 i - 20 j) m/s.
steps: Use the vertical condition Delta y=-20=0*t-0.5(10)t^2, giving t=2 s.
v_x=15 m/s and v_y=-10(2)=-20 m/s at impact.

repair.action: For any unequal-height landing, use the actual Delta y=y_f-y_i in the vertical position equation and retain the actual u_y; for a horizontal launch specifically, set u_y=0, then obtain the event time vertically and share it with x.
repair.why_valid: Initial vertical velocity and landing displacement describe different facts. The landing event is fixed by the actual vertical geometry, while u_y=0 is only the horizontal-launch initial condition.
repair.output: Delta y=y_f-y_i=u_y t_event-0.5g t_event^2; for horizontal launch u_y=0; reuse the solved t_event on x
